activities.anchor: The two epics are the tradition's first great audit of that economy
activities.caption: drag the divider across the two epics
activities.name: homAuditCompare

config.prompt: One heroic universe, read from both ends — drag the divider:

before.label: the Iliad
before.text: Rage at full power: honour (time) as a finite currency, a quarrel unanswerable inside the code, and the cost counted — a few weeks of the war's tenth year ending in shared grief, not victory.

after.label: the Odyssey
after.text: The code revalued from home: metis beats force, xenia defines civilisation, and the real tests are domestic — Penelope's weaving, the marriage bed rooted in an olive tree.

config.why: One epic prices the currency, the other asks what survives when it is gone — the same world read from both ends.

activities.anchor: That detail is a much later invention
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the heel and other inventions
activities.name: homHeelSpot

config.prompt: A student retells the Achilles story. One line is wrong — click it:
lines: The Iliad's first word is menin — rage — and the subject is one hero's fury, not the Trojan War.
Achilles chose between two fates: a long life at home without glory, or a short life at Troy with kleos forever.
In Homer, Achilles is fully mortal — nothing is pre-decided by magic anatomy.
His one weakness is the heel: dipped in the Styx by his mother, invulnerable everywhere but where she held him.
The poem ends with Priam and Achilles weeping together — a tragedy of the victors.
config.correction: The heel is a Roman-era add-on — Statius supplied the Styx-dipping; in Homer the choice, and the death, carry their weight unassisted.
config.why: Subtract the heel and the code comes back into focus: kleos bought with a real death.

activities.anchor: The poem's structure sets its values
activities.caption: put the Odyssey's three movements in order
activities.name: homStructOrder

config.prompt: Put the Odyssey's three movements in order:
items: Books 1–4: Telemachus, the son, learning to act
Books 5–12: Odysseus narrates his own wanderings — the Cyclops, Circe, the Sirens, the land of the dead
Books 13–24: the return in disguise, the bow contest, the slaughter and reunion
config.why: The shape is the argument: the son grows up first, the wanderer tells his own tale, and home gets the last word.

activities.anchor: And the poem's moral centre is domestic
activities.caption: pair each figure with the virtue they are measured by
activities.name: homVirtueMatch

config.prompt: Pair each figure with the virtue they are measured by:

pairs.right: force — the greatest warrior alive, whose rage organises the Iliad
metis — cunning intelligence, the trick that wins when strength cannot
fidelity — unravelling her weaving nightly for three years
duty — the farewell on the wall before a battle he knows he will lose

config.why: The two epics measure worth in different coin — and the household's tests turn out to be the harder ones.

activities.caption: walk up to two doors — how does each household receive you?
activities.name: homXeniaBranch

config.root: You arrive, exhausted, at a stranger's threshold. The custom of the sea decides how you are received — walk the two households.

start.text: The entrance opens. Which household have you found?

choices.label: A lord who asks who you are — only after food and drink
choices.feedback: The civilised order: the stranger is fed before questions, gifts follow, and the host earns reputation by it.

choices.label: A one-eyed giant who eats two of your crew
choices.feedback: The counter-case: the guest-eater defines the value by its absence — no laws, no assemblies, no welcome.

good.text: Fed first, questioned after, sent off with gifts — the bargain every civilised threshold keeps.

bad.text: The cave of the one-eyed giant: the anti-home. Escape is metis' job — the name 'Nobody', the stake, the rams.

config.why: Every doorway reports whether the household is civilised by its treatment of the stranger — and the guest-eater defines the value by its absence.

activities.caption: file each repetition by the machine that runs it
activities.name: homRepSort

config.prompt: Two machines run under the repetition — file each example:

items.label: 'Swift-footed Achilles' — even when he is sitting down
rosy-fingered Dawn, returning book after book
the arming scene, unfolding in a standard block
the feast or the sacrifice, assembled and varied like musical phrases
the arrival at a stranger's threshold

config.why: Metrically shaped phraseology and standard blocks are the machinery of live composition — the singer assembles fluent verse in real time.

activities.anchor: the way a novelist writes a novel
activities.caption: true or false — separating the poems from the legends
activities.name: homAuthorJudge

statements.s: The Iliad ends with the wooden horse and the fall of Troy.
statements.why: It ends with Hector's funeral — the war unfinished; the horse belongs to other traditions and appears in the Odyssey as a tale told at a feast.

statements.s: Homer's Achilles is invulnerable except for his heel.
statements.why: A Roman-era addition — in Homer he is fully mortal, which is exactly what gives his choice its weight.

statements.s: The Odyssey is a homecoming told in flashes, where the monsters matter less than whether a marriage can survive.
statements.why: The shape is the values: the wanderings are narrated by Odysseus himself, in the central books.

statements.s: The poems were composed alone, with a pen, once.
statements.why: They are the crystallised peak of a centuries-old singing tradition, fixed by writing in the eighth to sixth centuries BCE.
